paragraphs: In model-based reinforcement learning, a learned policy can help a planner explore by proposing promising actions. But the planner ultimately determines which actions generate training data. If the policy is updated independently, the two can drift apart, making value estimates less reliable and harming performance over longer horizons.

The paper introduces Policy Optimization–Model Predictive Control, or PO-MPC, to organize methods that keep these components aligned. Its central idea is to use the planner’s action distribution as a prior when optimizing the policy. KL regularization measures and penalizes distributional disagreement, connecting policy updates to the behavior of the planner that supplies their data.

This framework recovers existing approaches as special cases and identifies additional variants that had not previously been studied. Experiments show significant performance improvements from these variants within MPPI-based reinforcement learning. The contribution is both conceptual and practical: a shared mathematical formulation explains related methods and provides a systematic way to develop stronger combinations of learned policies and planning.
icml-2026-a-kl-regularization-framework-.tldr: PO-MPC unifies planner-aligned policy learning through KL regularization and produces variants that improve MPPI-based reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Sequential hypothesis tests decide whether to keep collecting observations or stop and draw a conclusion. This paper studies that decision when observations come from an ergodic Markov chain with finitely many states. The hypotheses concern whether its unknown transition matrix belongs to one prescribed collection of matrices or a separate alternative collection.

The authors derive a lower bound on the expected time any valid test needs to stop under the alternative. Unlike a purely asymptotic statement, this bound applies before taking a limiting regime. It also depends on the particular chain, incorporating both how often states are visited in the long run and how transitions connect those states.

They then construct a test whose expected stopping time approaches this bound as the permitted error level tends to zero. This establishes optimality in that limit, rather than claiming exact optimality at every error level. Applications include detecting misspecified Markov Chain Monte Carlo models and testing properties of transition dynamics in Markov decision processes.
icml-2026-asymptotically-optimal-sequent.tldr: The paper derives a sharp stopping-time bound for Markov-dependent hypothesis testing and constructs a test that attains it asymptotically.

paragraphs: Policies for controlling network spread can perform poorly when realistic randomness replaces simplified training dynamics. The paper identifies three causes: deterministic approximations underrepresent variability, aggregated observations hide highly influential nodes, and critics that predict only average outcomes struggle with cascades that tend either to die out or become widespread.

The proposed observer groups nodes by influence level, retaining information about hubs while keeping computation linear in the number of nodes. Its observations have a fixed dimension, allowing the policy to transfer across network sizes and topologies. A second component uses distributional reinforcement learning with Truncated Quantile Critics to represent outcome variability and improve risk-aware decisions.

Training uses a GPU-accelerated simulator with non-Markovian renewal dynamics, allowing spreading behavior beyond the Markovian simplifications under study. The authors report a 59-fold improvement over Markovian baselines and robust zero-shot transfer to Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube networks. Together, the findings support preserving influential-node structure and outcome distributions when learning policies for stochastic spreading processes.
icml-2026-closing-the-sim-to-real-gap-in.tldr: Influence-aware observations and distributional reinforcement learning improve control of stochastic network cascades and transfer across network settings.

paragraphs: Genomic models face a tradeoff between preserving DNA structure and processing long sequences efficiently. Subword tokenization can split meaningful biological patterns, while treating every nucleotide separately becomes computationally expensive. dnaHNet addresses this by learning how to group the sequence as part of the same process that learns to predict it.

The model starts from raw nucleotides and uses differentiable dynamic chunking to create compressed latent tokens. These groupings adapt to the sequence, balancing the amount of compression against predictive accuracy. Recursive chunking builds a hierarchy, so the model can represent genomic information at multiple levels without relying on a separate, fixed tokenizer.

Pretrained on prokaryotic genomes, dnaHNet is reported to outperform leading architectures, including StripedHyena2, in scaling and efficiency. The authors report quadratic FLOP reductions and more than threefold inference speedup over Transformers. They also find stronger zero-shot predictions of protein variant fitness and gene essentiality, alongside unsupervised discovery of hierarchical biological structure. These results connect computational compression with useful genomic representations.
icml-2026-dnahnet-a-scalable-and-hierarc.tldr: dnaHNet learns hierarchical DNA chunks directly from nucleotides, improving computational efficiency and zero-shot genomic prediction.

paragraphs: A language model deployed for a particular domain can still receive requests outside that domain. Detecting those inputs matters for keeping interactions within the provider’s intended scope. This paper investigates whether the model’s internal processing supplies useful evidence about domain membership, beyond methods that treat the model as a black box.

The approach represents internal activity using sparse autoencoders and examines how those representations change between layers. Rather than relying only on a single representation, it learns from transitions in the processing of an input. The authors present several lightweight ways to extract domain-specific signatures from these internal dynamics and distinguish out-of-domain text.

Experiments with the 2B and 9B versions of Gemma-2 support the usefulness of these transition-based representations. The analysis also aims to make the model’s evolving treatment of an input more interpretable, helping explain its decisions. The stated contribution concerns detecting domain boundaries through internal signals; it shows that layer-to-layer changes capture fine-grained input information relevant to that task.
icml-2026-domain-restriction-via-multi-s.tldr: Sparse-autoencoder representations of changes between language-model layers provide useful signatures for detecting out-of-domain inputs.

paragraphs: Neural controlled differential equations model sequences through a continuous path built from observations. The shape of that path affects computational cost: high-frequency variations from standard spline interpolation can force an adaptive numerical solver to take many small steps. More steps mean more evaluations of the model and slower inference.

The paper replaces exact interpolation with kernel smoothing and Gaussian process smoothing, giving explicit control over how regular the path becomes. Smoothing can remove useful detail, so the authors also introduce an attention-based multi-view model and a convolutional extension. Learnable queries guide path reconstruction, spreading representational capacity across several trajectories that capture different temporal patterns.

The resulting approach combines smoother inputs to the solver with multiple views that help recover information smoothing would otherwise discard. In the reported experiments, the convolutional multi-view model with Gaussian process smoothing achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while reducing both function evaluations and total inference time relative to spline-based baselines. The findings show that path construction can improve prediction and computational efficiency together.
icml-2026-efficient-neural-controlled-di.tldr: Smoother, attention-guided input paths improve neural CDE accuracy while reducing solver evaluations and inference time in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A kernel matrix records similarities between pairs of data points, so working through its entries can become expensive as the dataset grows. This paper develops approximate linear algebra algorithms that access such matrices through kernel density estimation queries. These queries provide a different route to information than reading individual matrix entries.

The algorithms improve matrix-vector products, matrix-matrix products, spectral-norm estimation, and estimation of the sum of all entries for Gaussian and other kernels. Their runtimes are linear in the input dimension and subquadratic in the number of points, with polynomial dependence on the requested accuracy. The improvements particularly reduce how quickly computational cost grows as tighter error tolerances are requested.

For Gaussian spectral-norm estimation, the reported exponent on inverse error decreases from about 7.7 to about 3.2. The entry-sum algorithm also improves dependence on dataset size. Alongside these upper bounds, the paper establishes lower bounds for related problems, including conditional quadratic-time hardness results. Those results help identify where density-estimation access may have limits despite its substantial algorithmic benefits.
icml-2026-even-faster-kernel-matrix-line.tldr: Kernel density estimation enables faster approximate kernel-matrix operations, especially by reducing their computational dependence on accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper seeks a theory of k-means clustering that better reflects practical datasets than worst-case analysis. Instead of assuming properties of an unknown optimal clustering, it assumes that high-dimensional observations concentrate around a lower-dimensional manifold. This shifts attention toward geometric properties of the data that can be examined empirically.

Using optimum quantization theory, the authors identify geometric scaling laws tied to intrinsic dimension. They exploit those regularities in Qkmeans, a fast method for selecting initial cluster centers. An input parameter controls a tradeoff between runtime and approximation quality, while intrinsic dimension affects the exponent in part of the computational cost.

The stated runtime includes a term proportional to the number of points, ambient dimension, and logarithm of the number of clusters, plus an additional cluster-dependent term. Its approximation guarantee also depends on the tradeoff parameter. A large empirical study across domains examines both the predicted scaling behavior and algorithm performance. The contribution connects a concrete geometric assumption to tunable guarantees for practical clustering initialization.
icml-2026-fast-k-means-seeding-under-the.tldr: Qkmeans uses geometric scaling laws under the manifold hypothesis to offer new speed–quality tradeoffs for k-means initialization.

paragraphs: Methods for interpreting language-model activations often look for a single direction associated with a concept. That geometric picture can miss concepts whose representations bend across activation space or require several dimensions. This paper explores a richer description in which the relevant structure depends on the local region of activation space.

The authors use a Mixture of Factor Analyzers, an unsupervised model that represents activations through Gaussian regions and their local covariance structure. Each activation is decomposed into a region’s center and variation around that center. This separates where an activation lies from how it varies locally, allowing multiple regional subspaces to describe more complex structures.

Large-scale models fitted to Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B capture nonlinear activation structure. On localization and steering benchmarks, the approach beats unsupervised baselines, competes with supervised localization methods, and often steers more effectively than sparse autoencoders. These results support local subspaces as useful objects for discovering concepts and controlling model behavior, extending analysis beyond isolated global directions.
icml-2026-from-directions-to-regions-dec.tldr: Modeling activations as locally structured regions improves concept localization and often strengthens steering compared with direction-based alternatives.

paragraphs: An evaluation observes only a sample of a model’s behavior, so sufficiently rare actions could escape detection. This paper tests a capability relevant to that possibility: whether models can deliberately take an action at a very low requested probability. Calibration means that repeated sampling produces approximately the requested frequency, rather than merely making the action uncommon.

The experiments prompt GPT-5, Claude 4.5, and Qwen-3 families with rates supplied directly or requiring derivation. With randomness available in context, such as a UUID, models remain well calibrated at rates as low as one in 100,000 actions. Without external randomness, some reach rates below one in 10,000. Larger models handle lower supplied rates more successfully.

A substantial qualification appears when models must derive the optimal rate: all tested models fail to calibrate without randomness or a hint to generate it. Successful strategies also reveal explicit reasoning, potentially enabling chain-of-thought monitoring. The findings establish a capability relevant to oversight, while the suggested risk to future evaluations remains conditional on scaling and the visibility of reasoning.
icml-2026-frontier-models-can-take-actio.tldr: Frontier models can accurately execute extremely rare actions under some conditions, exposing a potential weakness of limited-sample evaluations.

paragraphs: Equivariance means that transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation of the output. A network can have this property as a whole, but the relationship to symmetry inside its individual layers is less obvious. The paper asks when an overall equivariant function can also be represented through equivariant intermediate computations.

The main theorem assumes an appropriate form of parameter identifiability. Under that assumption, an end-to-end equivariant network admits a parameter choice implementing the same function whose layers are equivariant under suitable transformations of their hidden spaces. This is an existence result about an equivalent parameterization; it does not require every parameterization of the function to visibly exhibit those layerwise symmetries.

The argument uses an abstract, architecture-independent formalism. Existing identifiability results make it applicable immediately to a large class of networks, while application to other classes depends on still-conjectural identifiability properties. The theory offers a mathematical explanation for equivariant structure observed in trained weights, connecting symmetry at the input-output level with symmetry that can exist throughout the network.
icml-2026-identifiable-equivariant-netwo.tldr: Under an identifiability assumption, an equivariant network function admits an equivalent parameterization with equivariant individual layers.

paragraphs: Efficient sequence models can process long inputs with linear computational complexity, but they may struggle to maintain the expressive state representations needed for reasoning. This paper approaches sequence modeling through Bayesian filtering: maintaining a belief about the current state together with explicit uncertainty about that belief as observations arrive.

Classical Kalman filtering is usually treated as a sequential computation. The authors show that expressing it in information form turns its updates into an associative scan, a structure that permits parallel computation across time during training. Their Kalman Linear Attention layer therefore combines probabilistic state tracking with efficient parallel execution, while providing more expressive nonlinear updates and gating than the GLA variants considered.

Experiments report that KLA matches or exceeds modern state-space models and gated linear attention on discrete token manipulation, state tracking, and zero-shot commonsense reasoning benchmarks. The work also pretrains stacked Bayesian-filtering components at billion-token scale. Its central contribution is making explicit uncertainty tracking compatible with the computational advantages that motivate efficient alternatives to Transformers.
icml-2026-kalman-linear-attention-parall.tldr: Kalman Linear Attention reformulates Bayesian filtering for parallel training, combining explicit uncertainty tracking with efficient, expressive sequence modeling.

paragraphs: Lion and Muon are deep-learning optimizers, while stochastic Frank-Wolfe is a classical approach to constrained optimization. This paper connects them by showing that Lion and Muon with weight decay can be interpreted as instances of stochastic Frank-Wolfe. The connection supplies a common mathematical language for analyzing their behavior.

The authors establish convergence guarantees using the Frank-Wolfe gap, a measure of stationarity suited to constrained nonconvex problems. They further show that convergence in this measure implies convergence to a Karush–Kuhn–Tucker point for the corresponding norm-constrained problem. This characterizes a constrained stationarity condition, rather than asserting that the optimizers necessarily reach a globally best solution.

The paper also develops two robust stochastic Frank-Wolfe variants for heavy-tailed gradient noise, where unusually large gradient fluctuations matter. Their theoretical guarantees apply to general compact convex constraint sets without requiring large batches. Through the earlier connection, these developments yield new Lion and Muon variants designed to better accommodate heavy-tailed noise, expanding the conditions under which the optimization framework can be used.
icml-2026-lions-and-muons-optimization-v.tldr: A stochastic Frank-Wolfe interpretation gives convergence guarantees for Lion and Muon and motivates variants robust to heavy-tailed gradient noise.

paragraphs: Long reasoning traces contain changes in strategy that are difficult to understand by examining individual tokens alone. This paper approximates those dynamics with a finite-state machine containing six abstract cognitive states. The authors show that the states and their transitions can be captured in the model’s latent representations.

Analyzing the transition structure reveals statistical differences between reasoning chains that succeed and those that fail. The paper then uses this representation for training-free inference control. Its Q-value-guided steering estimates the longer-term usefulness of state transitions and applies sparse, orthogonal activation interventions at sentence boundaries, treating the direction of reasoning as a planning problem.

Across AIME25, MATH-500, GSM8k, and GPQA Diamond with three open reasoning models, the method produces significant performance gains. It often needs 25 times fewer interventions than greedy and weighted baselines. These findings suggest that guiding higher-level reasoning transitions can be effective and economical. The finite-state representation remains an approximation of the models’ emerging dynamics, rather than a complete description of their reasoning.
icml-2026-modeling-hierarchical-thinking.tldr: A six-state approximation of reasoning dynamics enables training-free steering that improves benchmark performance with relatively few interventions.

paragraphs: A request may need several kinds of expertise within the same response, such as mathematics and programming, or text and image generation. Assigning the entire sequence to one specialized adapter forces a single choice. This paper instead routes individual tokens, allowing different parts of a sequence to use different adapters.

Routing can follow vocabulary structure for multimodal models or a learned gate for semantic specialization. MoLoRA uses the latter idea to compose independently trained LoRA adapters at inference time. For the mixed-adapter setting analyzed, the paper establishes work proportional to the number of tokens, compared with replaying the sequence once per adapter in the per-sequence systems it considers.

In experiments across four reasoning benchmarks, MoLoRA makes Qwen3-1.7B outperform Qwen3-8B despite being 4.7 times smaller. This is evidence that combining focused specialization can surpass a larger model in those evaluations. The proposed workflow also supports loading independently trained adapters together without retraining them and extending available expertise by adding adapters, making specialization modular at inference time.
icml-2026-molora-composable-specializati.tldr: MoLoRA routes tokens among specialized adapters, combining expertise efficiently and enabling a smaller model to outperform a larger one on four reasoning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Language models commonly learn from a broad corpus before continuing training on specialized data. When several domains are involved, this creates a resource-allocation question: how much computation should go toward general pretraining, and how much toward each model’s specialization? The paper develops a scaling-law approach to guide that division.

The proposed method considers multiple models pretrained independently on a general corpus and then trained further for specialized domains. It predicts model loss using three quantities: model size, the number of general pretraining tokens, and the number of specialization tokens. These predictions provide a basis for selecting the compute allocation between the two training stages.

The authors report that the resulting loss model extrapolates to larger models and larger token budgets. Applied to language-model training, the allocation approach consistently improves common-sense knowledge and reasoning benchmark performance across the tested model sizes and compute budgets. The practical contribution is a predictive way to plan specialization, linking training-stage budgets to expected performance instead of treating the split as a fixed recipe.
icml-2026-optimal-splitting-of-language-.tldr: Scaling laws predict specialized-model loss and guide compute allocation between general pretraining and domain-specific continued training.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning on difficult reasoning problems can spend substantial computation producing unsuccessful solutions, leaving little useful learning signal. PrefixRL reuses successful traces obtained earlier by providing the beginning of a solution and letting the current model complete it. The supplied prefix makes an otherwise difficult problem more accessible.

The prefix comes from off-policy data, but the continuation is generated and trained with on-policy reinforcement learning. This avoids directly using old traces as supervision targets. Changing prefix length adjusts difficulty and the availability of successful continuations. The authors prove consistency with the standard reinforcement-learning objective and greater sample efficiency for the PrefixRL objective.

Empirically, training on prefixed problems improves performance even when prefixes are removed, and learned strategies often differ from those supplied. The experiments obtain successful traces through rejection sampling with the base model. Including that initial sampling cost, PrefixRL reaches the same training reward twice as fast as the strongest baseline, supervised training on off-policy data followed by RL, and achieves three times the final reward.
icml-2026-reuse-your-flops-scaling-rl-on.tldr: PrefixRL reuses successful solution prefixes to strengthen on-policy learning on hard problems and improves performance even without prefixes at evaluation.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based text generation must reconcile continuous changes during diffusion with the discrete choice of words or tokens. Existing approaches make different compromises. Continuous embedding spaces retain semantic relationships but complicate decoding, while categorical representations respect token discreteness without naturally capturing how tokens relate in meaning.

Smoothie proposes a diffusion space built by progressively smoothing token embeddings according to semantic similarity. This creates a way to remove information gradually while retaining a natural route back to discrete tokens. The method aims to combine the semantic organization of embeddings with the decoding advantages of representations that explicitly accommodate token choices.

Experiments cover both sequence-to-sequence generation, where text is generated from an input sequence, and unconditional generation. Smoothie improves generation quality over the existing diffusion-based models evaluated. Ablation studies also compare diffusion spaces and find the proposed space performs better than standard embeddings and the categorical simplex. These comparisons support the choice of diffusion representation as a meaningful contributor to the reported gains in text generation.
icml-2026-smoothie-smoothing-diffusion-o.tldr: Smoothie uses semantic smoothing of token embeddings to improve diffusion-based text generation while preserving a natural decoding process.

paragraphs: A model that predicts physical solutions must account for the shape of the domain and the boundary conditions imposed on it. Geo-NeWF addresses generalization to unfamiliar geometries by combining learning with a finite element method. It jointly learns a differential operator and compatible reduced spaces in which solutions are represented.

Geometry enters twice: a transformer encodes the discretized mesh, and that mesh also provides the basis for the learned finite element spaces. The resulting model is solved to obtain predictions. Finite Element Exterior Calculus makes physical conservation laws hold exactly, while a new constitutive-model parameterization ensures that the solution exists and is unique.

This construction directly ties predictions to geometry, boundary conditions, and mathematical structure rather than leaving those relationships entirely to data fitting. On several steady-state PDE benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and substantial improvements over conventional baselines on out-of-distribution geometries. The results support structure-preserving learning as a way to improve geometric generalization while retaining conservation properties in the computed solutions.
icml-2026-structure-preserving-learning-.tldr: Geo-NeWF combines learned finite element spaces with exact conservation structure to improve PDE prediction on unseen geometries.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings from descriptions of physical problems to their solutions, but unfamiliar conditions or dynamics can undermine their predictions. Fine-tuning can address this only when examples from the new dynamics are available. This paper investigates adapting the computation at test time while leaving pretrained model weights unchanged.

The method builds on DISCO, a dictionary of neural operators trained on different dynamics. At test time, it searches for compositions of these existing operators that approximate an unseen system. Operator splitting supplies the compositional strategy: available learned pieces are combined to represent dynamics beyond those individually encountered during training.

On out-of-distribution tasks involving parameter extrapolation and new combinations of physical phenomena, the authors report state-of-the-art zero-shot generalization. The approach can also recover underlying PDE parameters in the studied setting. These findings suggest that additional test-time search can make a pretrained operator collection more flexible, with adaptation taking place through the choice and composition of operators rather than through changes to their learned weights.
icml-2026-test-time-generalization-for-p.tldr: Searching over compositions of pretrained neural operators improves zero-shot prediction of unseen physical dynamics without changing model weights.

paragraphs: A distribution-shift detector compares arriving observations with what normal data should look like. Standard conformal test martingales continually enlarge their reference set. After a shift, however, changed observations enter that set and make the new behavior appear less unusual, weakening evidence and potentially delaying detection.

The paper instead compares every incoming sample with a fixed dataset representing the null distribution. Keeping that reference unchanged prevents post-shift contamination, but a finite reference set estimates the null distribution imperfectly. The main technical contribution is a robust martingale construction that explicitly accounts for this estimation error and remains valid conditional on the observed reference data.

The construction provides anytime-valid type-I error control, so repeatedly checking for an alarm preserves the stated false-alarm guarantee. It also comes with asymptotic power-one and bounded expected detection-delay guarantees. Experiments show faster detection than standard conformal test martingales. The work therefore addresses both the statistical validity of a fixed-reference approach and the practical loss of sensitivity caused by updating references after a change.
icml-2026-testing-for-distribution-shift.tldr: A fixed-reference conformal detector avoids contamination after distribution shifts while retaining anytime-valid false-alarm control.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning can improve a language model on a target task while eroding other capabilities. This paper attributes that forgetting to supervision mismatch: fixed training labels become increasingly misaligned with the model’s changing policy. Reinforcement learning generally retains broader capabilities better, but introduces reward-design, stability, and sampling costs.

Trajectory-Mixed Supervision creates a changing curriculum from the model’s own earlier checkpoints. This reward-free self-distillation framework seeks to reduce Policy-Label Divergence, the discrepancy between the evolving policy and its supervision. The authors connect reducing that discrepancy with preventing the mode collapse responsible for forgetting in standard supervised fine-tuning.

Across mathematics reasoning and instruction-following evaluations, TMS improves the tradeoff between task accuracy and retention of existing capabilities. It significantly outperforms standard and iterative supervised fine-tuning, although reinforcement learning remains strongest for retention. Mechanistic analysis finds that divergence drift predicts forgetting and that TMS reduces this drift. The findings support adapting supervision over training as a way to approach RL’s retention benefits without reward models or verifiers.
icml-2026-tms-trajectory-mixed-supervisi.tldr: TMS uses historical model checkpoints to adapt supervision, improving task learning and capability retention without rewards or verifiers.

paragraphs: A model can represent a world with several underlying factors by tracking all their combinations or by representing the factors separately. The first strategy requires a space that grows exponentially with the number of parts; the second uses orthogonal subspaces whose total dimension grows linearly. This paper formalizes those two representational possibilities.

Both representations can track uncertainty about hidden factors given the current context. However, separating factors loses fidelity when they are not conditionally independent. The authors derive distinct geometric predictions for the two hypotheses, including how many subspaces should appear, their dimensions, and how context representations should be arranged within them.

Tests use Transformers trained on synthetic processes with known hidden structure. With conditionally independent factors, the models learn factored representations. When noise or dependencies disrupt that structure, their effective dimensionality gradually grows during training to recover fidelity. These results explain factorization in the studied setting and suggest that interpretable low-dimensional structure may also persist in models trained on more complex data.
icml-2026-transformers-learn-factored-re.tldr: Synthetic-process experiments show Transformers separating independent latent factors into orthogonal subspaces and expanding dimensionality when dependencies demand richer representations.

paragraphs: Cellular processes evolve at very different speeds, from changes in gene expression to protein abundance and metabolic activity. Those differences create stiffness, which can make standard neural differential equations difficult to train stably. Discrete sequence models can also inadequately represent interactions across these time scales and miss brief responses.

The proposed Tri-Scale Stiff NODE uses hierarchically coupled latent differential equations to model relationships from genes to proteins and metabolites. Training combines reconstruction error with an information-theoretic mutual-information objective. Its continuous-time representation is intended to identify disease dynamics and drug perturbations acting within narrow windows that discrete-time approaches may overlook.

Lyapunov analysis provides a theoretical guarantee that modeled trajectories remain stable and well behaved even under extreme stiffness. The authors validate the methodology on the STATegra B-cell and Traxler macrophage datasets, using STATegra for a proof-of-concept drug-repurposing pipeline. The work links a stability-focused mathematical design with multi-omics modeling, while the drug-repurposing component is presented as a computational proof of concept.
icml-2026-tri-scale-neural-odes-for-cont.tldr: Hierarchically coupled neural ODEs model gene, protein, and metabolic dynamics across time scales with theoretical stability under extreme stiffness.

paragraphs: A generative model can reveal whether an example was in its training data without reproducing that example in its outputs. This paper studies such membership signals in flow matching. It examines reconstruction behavior along the linear interpolation path used in training, rather than looking only at final generated samples.

The authors find that the reconstruction gap between training and test examples traces a bell-shaped curve along this path. The gap accumulates during training even while validation metrics remain stable. Under Gaussian assumptions, they derive a closed-form prediction for where the signal reaches its maximum, identifying a specific part of the path where membership evidence is strongest.

Experiments on audio and images validate the bell-shaped structure, while the predicted peak location holds when the stated assumptions are satisfied. A proof-of-concept membership-inference attack exploits this location-dependent signal to distinguish training examples from nonmembers. The findings show how apparently stable validation behavior can coexist with increasing traces of training membership, and why examining the interpolation path reveals information that output reproduction alone would miss.
icml-2026-where-flow-matching-leaks-char.tldr: Flow-matching reconstruction errors expose a bell-shaped membership signal along the training interpolation path that can support membership-inference attacks.
